120.title: Om jai jagadish hare
120.hook: Gajendra calls on Hari from the crocodile's grip; the arti song sings that rescue
120.carry: hari, the one who takes the trouble away
120.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes and temples, especially in North India and the diaspora, Om jai jagadish hare is sung while the arti lamp is circled at the end of puja, with a bell ringing and everyone joining in.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Narada's monkey face: camphor burns bright and leaves no ash. Your line was burn the ego like camphor.

segments.voice: A lake high on a mountain, thick with lotuses. The king of the elephants, Gajendra, wades in with his whole herd to bathe. Then something grabs his leg. A crocodile, and it won't let go. He pulls toward the shore; it pulls toward the deep. His family try to drag him out and can't. In the telling, the struggle goes on for years, and slowly the strongest animal on the mountain runs out of strength. His herd can't save him. There's one thing left he can do.
screen: `A LAKE, A HERD, A CROCODILE.` → `THE STRONGEST ONE IS STUCK.` → `ONE THING LEFT TO DO.`

segments.voice: This is Gajendra, from the Bhagavata Purana, one of the best-loved stories of Vishnu. Near the end, the elephant lifts a lotus in his trunk and prays. And notice how he prays. Most of it isn't begging. It's praise: you are the source of everything, the shelter of whoever turns to you. Only then does he ask. And Vishnu comes at once, cuts the crocodile away with his spinning discus, and pulls the elephant out of the water. Now listen to the song that's sung while the arti flame circles: Om jai jagadish hare. Jai, victory. Jagadish, lord of the world. Hare calls on Hari, a name of Vishnu that tradition explains as the one who takes away: takes away what has hold of you. The next lines say it plainly: the troubles of your devotees, you take away in a moment. That's Gajendra's story in one line. The song itself isn't ancient. It's usually credited to Shardha Ram Phillauri, a Punjabi writer of the eighteen-hundreds, and it's in Hindi, so anyone could understand it. But what it teaches is old. This is bhakti, loving devotion. Gajendra was the strongest one on the mountain, and strength ran out. What he had left was a name to call. Many teachers read the crocodile as whatever has hold of you that you can't pull free from alone. So the song starts with praise, jai, then remembers that people are hurting, and trusts Hari to come quickly.
screen: `GAJENDRA PRAISES, THEN ASKS.` · `HARI: THE ONE WHO TAKES AWAY.` · `A HINDI SONG, AN OLD TEACHING.` · `BHAKTI: A NAME TO CALL.`

segments.voice: Slowly, speak it, sing it or just listen inside: Om jai jagadish hare, swami jai jagadish hare. Once more, a little slower; if you'd like, let a flame or your open hand circle with the tune. Then name, silently, one thing that has hold of you right now, and lift it up the way the elephant lifted his lotus. If you don't pray, simply listen to the words and the tune, and let the sound settle.
Hari, a name of Vishnu, the one who takes away: the name Gajendra called from the lake, and the one the arti song calls, Om jai jagadish hare. Today's word.
screen: `HARI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Hari, the one who takes the trouble away. The elephant called, and help came at once. Day one hundred twenty, done.

121.title: Taking the light
121.hook: Krishna eats Sudama's handful of rice; why the arti flame comes back to everyone
121.carry: what you offer comes back as grace
121.howItsDone: At the end of arti, the lamp is brought to each person, who passes cupped hands over the flame without touching it and then touches the hands to the eyes, face or head; in temples, people often place a small offering on the plate as it passes.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hari, the one who takes the trouble away: the elephant called, and Vishnu came. Your line named him.

segments.voice: A poor man stands outside a palace gate in Dvaraka, holding a small bundle of flattened rice tied in a rag. His wife begged it from the neighbors. Inside lives Krishna, his old friend from school, now a king. Who brings a handful of rice to a king? But the gates open, and Krishna runs out, hugs him, washes his feet, and sits him on his own bed. Then he smiles and asks: so, what did you bring me?
screen: `A POOR MAN AT A PALACE GATE.` → `A HANDFUL OF RICE IN A RAG.` → `WHAT DID YOU BRING ME?`

segments.voice: The friend is usually called Sudama, and the story is in the Bhagavata Purana. Sudama hides the bundle. He's ashamed. Krishna takes it from him anyway, opens it, and eats a handful with delight, as if it were the best food in the palace. In the telling, he says he gladly accepts even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water, when it's offered with love. Sudama walks home without asking for a thing. When he gets there, his hut has become a house full of plenty. He gave a handful. It came back as grace. Hindus have a word for what comes back: prasad, grace. You met it with the laddus: food is offered at the shrine, then shared out as a blessing. Arti works the same way, with light. When the song ends, the lamp that was just circled before the divine is carried out to everyone. You cup your hands over the flame, close enough for warmth, never touching, then bring your hands to your eyes, your face, sometimes over your head. That's taking the light: receiving the blessing back. A few customs travel with it. An arti flame usually isn't blown out; blowing on a sacred flame is often seen as disrespectful. And if you're a guest and unsure, watch first, then copy the person beside you. The light is offered to everyone in the room, the way Krishna treated a poor friend's handful as a king's gift.
screen: `KRISHNA EATS THE RICE WITH DELIGHT.` · `PRASAD: WHAT COMES BACK IS GRACE.` · `HANDS OVER THE FLAME, THEN TO THE EYES.` · `DON'T BLOW IT OUT.`

segments.voice: If it's safe, light a candle or lamp; if not, picture the arti plate coming toward you. Cup your hands and pass them slowly over the warmth, a few inches above, never touching, then draw them back and rest your palms softly over your closed eyes, feeling the warmth there. Once more, and this time let your hands pass over the top of your head, then rest them in your lap and stay with the flame.
Jyoti, the flame: after arti it comes back out to the people, and hands pass over it to the eyes and the head, taking the light as grace. Today's word.
screen: `JYOTI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what you offer comes back as grace. Sudama gave a handful; the light comes back to your hands. Until tomorrow.

122.title: Family arti
122.hook: a meat-seller teaches a proud scholar that worship starts at home; why arti is a family thing
122.carry: a householder's home is holy ground
122.howItsDone: In many Hindu homes, evening arti is a family gathering: one person circles the lamp, a child often rings the bell, everyone sings, and the lamp is passed around so each person can take the light.

segments.voice: A young scholar sits under a tree, reciting the Vedas. A crane on the branch above makes a mess on his head. He glares up in anger, and the bird drops dead. That's how much power his discipline has given him. Shaken, he goes to beg for food at a house. The woman inside says, wait. Her husband has just come home tired and hungry, and she feeds him first. When she finally comes out, the scholar is furious. She answers calmly: I'm not a crane, you know.
screen: `A SCHOLAR, A CRANE, ONE ANGRY LOOK.` → `WAIT.` → `I'M NOT A CRANE, YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: The scholar is Kaushika, and the story is in the Mahabharata. Somehow the woman knows about the bird. She tells him: if you want to understand dharma, go to the city of Mithila and find a certain man who sells meat in the market. A meat-seller, teaching a scholar? Kaushika goes. The man looks up from his stall and says: the woman sent you. Then he takes Kaushika home and shows him what he calls his gods: his old mother and father, whom he feeds and cares for every day. That, he says, is his worship. Then the turn: you left your own parents to study, and they're grieving. Go home. And Kaushika does. This is grihastha dharma, the way of the householder. Hindu tradition names stages of life, and many paths honor the one who leaves home for the forest. But this story says the house itself can be holy ground. Feeding, caring, earning a living honestly: done as dharma, it's worship. That's why evening arti is so often a family thing. It has jobs. Someone holds the lamp. Someone rings the bell, often the youngest. Everyone sings and takes the light. Real families are complicated. Some people live alone, some with a partner from another faith or none. Nobody has to join; a guest can simply stand and listen. But the invitation is the point. The meat-seller's temple was a small house with two old people in it.
screen: `A MEAT-SELLER TEACHES A SCHOLAR.` · `HIS PARENTS ARE HIS WORSHIP.` · `GRIHASTHA: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `NO ONE HAS TO. EVERYONE IS ASKED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people you share a roof with, or the ones you'd call family wherever they are. Picture them in the room for arti, one holding the flame, one ringing the bell. Then pick one person, a roommate, a parent on a video call, a partner, a child, a friend, and think how you might invite them, once, simply, with no pressure at all; if they say no, that's fine too. If you don't pray, simply picture who you'd want at your table tonight.
Family arti: one lamp, one bell, one song, and a job for everyone in the house, the householder's worship done together. Today's word.

123.title: Sunset without objects
123.hook: Agastya teaches Rama a hymn to the sun mid-battle; worship needs no objects
123.carry: the sun is the god you can see
123.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the sun directly, pouring water toward it at dawn or bowing to it at the twilight junctions, and some recite the Aditya Hridayam; when no shrine is available, some simply face the rising or setting sun with folded hands.

segments.voice: The war in Lanka has gone on and on. Rama stands facing Ravana, and for once he's worn out, wondering how this fight can be won. There's no temple here. No lamp, no bell, no flowers. Just dust, arrows, and the sun overhead. Then an old sage makes his way across the battlefield to him: Agastya. Rama, he says, listen. I'll teach you something you can do right here, right now, with nothing in your hands.
screen: `A BATTLEFIELD. NO TEMPLE, NO LAMP.` → `A SAGE WALKS UP.` → `SOMETHING YOU CAN DO RIGHT HERE.`

segments.voice: In the Ramayana, what Agastya teaches is a hymn to the sun, the Aditya Hridayam, the heart of the sun. It praises the sun as the light in all the gods, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and more, and as the witness of everything people do. Rama looks toward the sun, recites the hymn, sips water three times to purify himself, and turns back to the fight with fresh strength. Soon after, Ravana falls. Here's the teaching. In Hindu tradition the sun is often called the god you can actually see. You don't need an image or a shelf to find him; he's in front of you every day, rising and setting. That's why so many Hindus pour water toward the sun at dawn, as you did on day one hundred fifteen, and why worship never depends on having the right objects. One way to see this week's arti lamp: every evening, as the sun goes down, a household lights a small flame and holds it up, a little sun carried indoors for the night. That's a reading, not a rule, but it means this: when you have nothing, you still have the original flame. Anywhere, you can turn west at dusk, put your hands together, and watch the light finish its path. One practical thing: never stare straight into the sun. Watch the sky around it, the colors, the edges of the clouds.
screen: `AGASTYA'S HYMN: THE HEART OF THE SUN.` · `THE GOD YOU CAN ACTUALLY SEE.` · `THE LAMP: A LITTLE SUN INDOORS.` · `FACE WEST. HANDS TOGETHER. WATCH.`

segments.voice: If you can, turn toward the west, toward a window or where the sun sets even if it's hidden right now; if it's not evening, picture the last sunset you remember well. Put your hands together at your chest if you'd like, and look at the sky around the sun, never at the sun itself. Let the color be the flame and the whole horizon the plate: nothing to hold, nothing to light, just the original flame and you in front of it.
Surya, the sun, honored as the god you can see: Rama prayed to him on a battlefield, and you can face him at dusk with nothing in your hands. Today's word.

124.title: Your evening routine
124.hook: Kavi gives King Nimi one line to end the day; offer everything, then build the evening routine
124.carry: hand the whole day back to god
124.howItsDone: Many Hindu households close the day with evening arti at the home shrine, and many close their prayers with a verse offering all one's actions to God (kayena vacha…, from the Bhagavata Purana) and Om shanti shanti shanti.

segments.voice: A king named Nimi is in the middle of a grand ceremony when nine wanderers walk in, brothers, bright as the sun, carrying nothing. Nimi stops everything, stands, and welcomes them with honor. Then he asks the question he's actually been carrying all his life: what is the best thing a person can do? The first brother, Kavi, answers, and the heart of his answer isn't a long ritual or a hard vow. It's one sentence, the kind you could say at the end of any day.
screen: `A KING, NINE WANDERERS.` → `WHAT'S THE BEST THING TO DO?` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Bhagavata Purana, and Kavi's sentence is still said in many Hindu homes, often at the close of puja or before sleep. In plain English it goes something like this: whatever I do, with my body, my words, my mind, my senses, my understanding, or simply out of my own nature, I offer it all to Narayana, to God. That's it. Not only the good things. Whatever I did. This is samarpana: offering, handing over. Krishna says much the same to Arjuna. The morning puja offers the day before it starts. The evening hands it back once it's done: the good, the hard, the moment you'd rather forget. You don't have to carry it into sleep, because it isn't only yours anymore. This week has given you the pieces. Put them together and you have an evening routine, about five minutes. First, the bell: one ring, followed all the way to silence. Second, the breath: in for four, out for six, a few rounds. Third, arti: circle a flame and take the light, or if there's no flame, face the window where the sun went down. And fourth, the offering: Kavi's line, in your own words, then Om shanti, shanti, shanti. This week an elephant, a poor friend, a meat-seller and a prince all ended up in the same place: handing something over to God. Tonight, it's your turn.

125.title: The body as temple
125.hook: Basavanna's poem and the Upanishad's line: the body is a shrine, so care is practice
125.carry: the body is a temple; someone holy lives here
125.howItsDone: Many Hindus bathe before morning puja and treat bodily care, food, rest and movement as part of religious life, drawing on the idea, found in later Upanishads and in devotional poetry, that the body is a temple in which the divine dwells.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, dinacharya, your evening routine, ending with an offering. Your line was hand the whole day back to God.
screen: `YOUR EVENING ROUTINE — HAND THE WHOLE DAY BACK TO GOD.`

segments.voice: For two weeks you've been building a shrine: a shelf, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a cup of water. You've learned to keep it clean, bring fresh flowers, light it at the edges of the day. Now look down. At your hands. Your feet. The chest going up and down. There's a shrine you've carried this whole time, one you didn't have to buy, and it's easy to treat it worse than the shelf. Meals get skipped, sleep gets cut, and it only gets noticed when it hurts. This week turns to the body and food. Today: the body as temple.
screen: `TWO WEEKS BUILDING A SHRINE.` → `NOW LOOK DOWN.` → `TODAY: THE BODY AS TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: A short line in the Maitreya Upanishad says it straight out: the body is called a temple, and the living one inside it is Shiva himself. The body is the building. What lives in it is holy. That's the teaching: the atman, the self within, is divine, so the body that houses it is a temple. You met atman on day ten: someone is in there. Today asks what that means for the building. Basavanna, a poet-saint of Karnataka who wrote in Kannada, put it in a poem that's still sung. The rich, he says, build temples for Shiva. What can a poor man do? Then he answers: my legs are the pillars, my body is the shrine, my head is the golden dome. He didn't need stone. He was already standing in one. So looking after the body isn't vanity, and it isn't a chore separate from the spiritual life. Bathing before puja, eating with some care, sleeping enough, moving, resting: these become part of the practice, the way sweeping the shrine is part of puja. And notice what the idea doesn't say. The temple doesn't have to be perfect, young or strong. It can be old, cracked, patched, or hard to climb the steps of. Bodies that are sick, tired, disabled or aging are still temples, and still lived in. The point is who lives there. This week is about caring for the building.
screen: `THE BODY IS CALLED A TEMPLE.` · `BASAVANNA: MY LEGS ARE THE PILLARS.` · `CARE IS PART OF THE PRACTICE.` · `A TEMPLE CAN BE OLD, OR CRACKED.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whatever's kinder today, and close your eyes if you like. Walk slowly through the temple: your feet, the foundation; the legs, Basavanna's pillars; the belly and chest, moving with the breath; the hands, which did so much work today; the shoulders, where the day usually hides; the face; the top of the head, the dome. Don't fix anything, just visit each part. Someone holy lives here.
Devalaya, a house of God: the old idea that the body itself is this shrine, with someone holy living in it, so caring for it is part of the practice. Today's word.

126.title: Sun salutation, plainly
126.hook: baby Hanuman leaps for the sun, then learns from it; the bow inside the yoga sequence
126.carry: surya namaskar is a bow to the sun
126.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice surya namaskar in the morning, facing east, as both exercise and devotion, sometimes reciting one of the twelve names of the sun, such as Om Mitraya namah, with each round.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-TWENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, devalaya: the body as a temple. Your line was the body is a temple; someone holy lives here.
screen: `THE BODY AS TEMPLE — SOMEONE HOLY LIVES HERE.`

segments.voice: A baby wakes up hungry and looks out at the sky. There, low on the horizon, is a huge, glowing, orange fruit. So he jumps for it. This is no ordinary baby. He's the son of the wind, and he flies straight up toward the rising sun, higher and higher. The gods panic. Indra, king of the gods, hurls his thunderbolt and strikes the child on the jaw, and he falls. The jaw, hanu in Sanskrit, gives him his name: Hanuman.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY. AN ORANGE FRUIT.` → `HE JUMPS FOR THE SUN.` → `HANU, THE JAW: HANUMAN.`

segments.voice: That's how the Ramayana tells it, and the story doesn't end with the fall. The wind god, his father, is so grieved that he stops blowing, and the gods have to heal the child and bless him. In later tellings, the boy who grabbed at the sun comes back to it as a student. Surya agrees to teach him, and Hanuman learns by moving across the sky, facing his teacher from sunrise to sunset. Grabbing at the sun, then bowing to it. Hindus honor the sun as the god you can see, and as a teacher of light. That's the bow in surya namaskar: surya, the sun, and namaskar, a bow, from the same root as namaste, your very first word. In its common form it's a flowing loop of about twelve positions, each with a breath. People who practice it as devotion often add what the gym leaves out: one of the sun's twelve names with each round. The first is Om Mitraya namah: a bow to Mitra, the friend. Now, plainly, the history. Honoring the sun is very old, but this flowing sequence was made popular in the early twentieth century by a raja in western India, for health. An old devotion in a fairly new shape. So in a yoga class it can be a stretch, and at home, facing east at dawn, it can be a bow. What makes it a salutation is who you have in mind.
screen: `HANUMAN GRABS AT THE SUN, THEN BOWS TO IT.` · `SURYA + NAMASKAR: A BOW TO THE SUN.` · `OM MITRAYA NAMAH: TO THE FRIEND.` · `OLD DEVOTION, FAIRLY NEW SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Three gentle rounds, standing or sitting tall, facing east if you know where it is; skip anything that hurts, or stay seated and just move your arms. Palms at your chest: breathe in and reach up, out and fold as far as is comfortable, in to lift halfway, out to fold, in to rise all the way up, arms high, out with palms back to the chest. Twice more, slowly, saying the friend's name with each round if you'd like, then sit and notice whatever warmth is there.
Surya namaskar. A bow to the sun: a flowing loop of positions, one breath each, done as exercise, as devotion, or both. Today's word.
